source.title: One Size Does Not Fit All: Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM
source.authors: Alessia Rossi; F. Campelo; Gabriel L. Oliveira

record.file_problem: The supplied paper text is substantially complete, including appendices; some figures are represented as text/flattened output.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares training loss and test accuracy for CAP-SAM, SAM, and SGD, and argues that better test performance can coexist with lower training loss, qualifying a simple flatness/generalization account. It does not test the listed memorization, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or example-removal versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper tests CAP-SAM against SAM and SGD on natural image labels, reporting test accuracy and training loss. It does not test random-label memorization, nor whether a measured trained-network property tracks the train–test gap. Results for the paper's proposed adaptive method versus other SAM variants are method comparisons; included only where the constant-versus-dynamic perturbation result bears on test performance. Cited prior results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization premise to develop CAP-SAM and reports optimizer performance. It does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps or test any other listed version. Lower training loss together with higher test accuracy does not challenge V7's correlational claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors conclude that adaptive perturbation radii improve accuracy across tested SAM variants, and report lower training loss than SAM with higher test accuracy. Improvements are aggregate rather than universal: CIFAR-10 VaSSO on WRN-28-10 and ImageNet SAM on Sketch decline. Their convergence-rate result requires a decaying radius, which is not the experimental update rule. Their interpretation invokes flatter minima, but they do not empirically establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sharpness-aware training with a dynamically adjusted perturbation radius (CAP-SAM), comparing it against fixed-radius SAM variants and SGD. Its experiments use standard image-classification training but do not match the original claim's random-label, width-sweep, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or example-removal methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that dynamic-radius gains vary by dataset, method, model, and test set: CIFAR-10 gains occur in 15 of 16 combinations; on ImageNet the stated exception is SAM on ImageNet-Sketch. Initial radius and growth factor meaningfully influence performance, while radius bounds have negligible impact. OOD test sets are separate from in-distribution ImageNet validation.

fits_no_version.finding: Dynamic SAM improves the recorded CIFAR accuracies and ImageNet-1K accuracy. On CIFAR-100, CAP-SAM has lower training loss than SAM and higher test accuracy than SAM and SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adapting SAM's perturbation radius can improve held-out image-classification performance while improving training fit relative to fixed-radius SAM.

fits_no_version.finding: Dynamic-radius variants improve mean accuracy in 11 of the 12 recorded additional ImageNet evaluations; SAM on Sketch decreases from 22.12% to 21.90%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of dynamic-radius SAM variants extend to additional ImageNet evaluation sets, with exceptions depending on method and test set.

record.peer_reviewed: OPT2026: 18th Annual Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning
record.problems: The generalization claim is supported by test accuracy and training-loss comparisons, not by a direct train–test gap analysis. Experiments use three independent runs. The theoretical convergence result assumes a decaying radius that the authors say is not used in experiments. Some figure curves are described textually without exact values. The paper's ImageNet OOD results do not bear on the in-distribution claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. OOD rows from Table 3 were retained because they are individually reported, but do not map to any claim version.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization, chance-level random-label test performance, and coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adam-style adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, weight-decay changes, or switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Association of magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance with train–test gaps at comparable training loss, and ranking against norm or margin measures. No such empirical analysis is reported.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows describe the proposed method's performance rather than evidence for V1–V8; cannot_determine denotes that mismatch, not unreadable accuracy values. The reported ± quantities are standard deviations over three runs. Aggregate significance tests do not establish significance for every individual row. No additional result bearing on a listed version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and chance-level random-label test accuracy; coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation on one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning and regularization recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
